1135.title: Principles six to nine
1135.hook: prophecy, Moses' unique prophecy, the Torah from heaven, and its permanence
1135.howItsDone: The Torah is read aloud from a handwritten scroll in the synagogue on Shabbat, Mondays, Thursdays and festivals, and read through in order, over a yearly cycle or, in some communities, a longer one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, principles one to five, all about God. Your line: one, bodiless, eternal. Today, the second stretch.

Two verses from the Torah. One: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The other is from a list of names in Genesis: the sons of Ham were Cush, and Mizraim, and Put, and Canaan. One you met yesterday, at the heart of Jewish prayer. The other is easy to skim. Is one of them holier than the other? Maimonides gives a blunt answer, and it sits at the center of today's four foundations: the ones about prophecy, and about the Torah itself.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` → `THE SONS OF HAM.` → `IS ONE HOLIER?`

segments.voice: Principles six to nine. The sixth: prophecy is real. God can speak to human beings, and some people, prepared and open, have heard. The seventh: the prophecy of Moses stands apart from every other. The Torah itself says so. In Numbers, God says that with other prophets He speaks in visions and dreams, but with Moses mouth to mouth, plainly, not in riddles. And at the end of Deuteronomy: no prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face. That's why the line from last week's saying, from Moses to Moses, carried such weight. The eighth: the Torah is from heaven. The whole Torah we have, Maimonides says, is the one given to Moses. And here is his blunt answer to the two verses. There is no difference, he says, between the sons of Ham and Hear, O Israel. Both come from the same source. Holiness isn't measured by how moving a verse sounds. The ninth: the Torah won't be replaced. Nothing will be added to it, and nothing taken away. Deuteronomy says it directly: "thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it." Put the four together and you get a chain. God speaks. Moses hears most clearly. What he receives is the Torah. And the Torah stays. Jews today hold the eighth and ninth in different ways, and that difference gets a day of its own soon. Prophecy and Torah.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the words that guide you most, from scripture, a parent or a teacher, and ask quietly where they reached you from. Follow the chain back, one link at a time, as far as you can. Then set the question down.

1136.title: Principles ten to thirteen
1136.hook: God knows, rewards and punishes, the messiah will come, the dead will live
1136.howItsDone: Some Jews recite the thirteen "I believe" lines, Ani Ma'amin, after the morning service; the twelfth line, about waiting for the messiah, is also sung to several melodies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prophecy and the Torah, every verse from the same source. Your line: prophecy and Torah. Today, the list's last stretch.

Thirteen lines, and every one opens the same way. I believe with complete faith. That's the shape of a version of Maimonides' list printed in prayer books, set out after the morning service. It isn't his own wording. Someone later recast each foundation as a sentence a person could say in the first person, out loud. So the list stops being a page of philosophy and becomes something said with the mouth. Today, the last four lines, the ones that look ahead.
screen: `THIRTEEN LINES, ONE OPENING.` → `I BELIEVE WITH COMPLETE FAITH.` → `THE LINES THAT LOOK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Principles ten to thirteen. The tenth: God knows what human beings do and think. Not in a general way, from far off. The Psalms say God fashions the hearts of all people and considers all their deeds. Nothing a person does falls outside God's notice. The eleventh: God rewards those who keep the commandments and punishes those who break them. Maimonides holds that the final reward is the world to come, the share this whole list began with. The twelfth: the messiah will come. And here the prayer-book version adds a phrase. Even though he may delay, I wait for him every day that he will come. Not a date on a calendar. A waiting that starts over each morning. The thirteenth: the dead will live again, at a time God chooses. That's the resurrection of the dead, a belief already present in the Mishnah chapter Maimonides was explaining. Now look at the whole list from here. It began with God, who has no beginning. It passed through prophecy and the Torah. And it ends with things that haven't happened yet. A creed that closes on hope rather than on a fact already settled. Some Jews say these lines each morning. Others study them, and argue with them, which is tomorrow. Each line still opens the same way. I believe with complete faith.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're waiting for, for yourself, for someone you love, or for the world: not a plan, a hope. The twelfth line waits every day without knowing the day; hold your hope that way for a few breaths, open and unhurried. If you pray, you can hold it before God.

1137.title: Not everyone agreed: Albo's three roots
1137.hook: Crescas and Albo proposed other lists; the streams read the principles differently
1137.carry: crescas and albo argued from inside, and stayed
1137.howItsDone: Jewish students read Maimonides' principles alongside the works of his critics, such as Crescas's Or Adonai and Albo's Sefer HaIkkarim; the different movements of Judaism explain in their own writings how they understand the principles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last four foundations, said in prayer books as I believe with complete faith. Today, the people who read the same list and answered back.

Three. Not thirteen. A Spanish rabbi named Joseph Albo read Maimonides' list carefully, with respect, and then wrote a whole book arguing that Judaism rests on three roots. Tradition says Albo studied with another sharp reader, Hasdai Crescas, who questioned the list from a different angle. Neither one walked away from Judaism. They stayed inside it and argued about its foundations. Today's lesson is in the title, and it's a habit this tradition keeps.
screen: `THREE, NOT THIRTEEN.` → `READ WITH RESPECT, ANSWERED BACK.` → `ARGUING FROM INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Not everyone agreed. Start with Crescas. In his book, The Light of the LORD, he asked a hard question about the very first principle. The Torah gives commandments. But can you command someone to believe God exists? A command already assumes someone is commanding. So for Crescas, God's existence is the ground the commandments stand on, not one more item among them. He sorted beliefs differently, into roots, foundations and true beliefs, not one flat list. Next, Albo. His book is called Sefer HaIkkarim, the Book of Roots. He kept many of Maimonides' ideas but counted only three roots: God exists, the Torah is from heaven, and there is reward and punishment. The others, he said, grow out of these, like branches from a trunk. Then, the streams today. Some Jews hold the thirteen as written, and say them as written. Some read certain lines, such as the dead living again or the Torah from heaven, in other ways. Some put practice and community at the center and hold belief more loosely. Each says why, from its own reading of the tradition. And notice one more thing. The arguers didn't throw the list away. They kept it on the table, so they could keep arguing with it. Agreeing on which questions matter can hold a people together, even when the answers differ. Not everyone agreed.
screen: `CRESCAS: CAN BELIEF BE COMMANDED?` · `ALBO: THREE ROOTS, NOT THIRTEEN.` · `THE STREAMS READ THE LIST DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE LIST STAYS ON THE TABLE.` · then, large: `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what you stand on: not what you're supposed to say, but what actually holds you up on a hard day. It might be a belief, a person, a promise, a practice; there's no right number, since Maimonides counted thirteen and Albo three. Rest on what you find.

1138.title: Eight Chapters
1138.hook: his introduction to Pirkei Avot, on the soul's health
1138.howItsDone: Shemonah Perakim is studied as an introduction to Pirkei Avot, a text some communities read chapter by chapter on Shabbat afternoons between Passover and Shavuot, and some through the summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the critics who counted differently. Your line: not everyone agreed. Today, back to Maimonides, and another doorway in his commentary.

Sweet tastes bitter. Bitter tastes sweet. A person with a sick body, Maimonides writes, can lose their sense of taste so badly that they crave what harms them and turn away from what would heal them. He knew bodies. He worked as a physician. But in this passage he isn't writing about the body. He's writing about the soul. And he says the same thing happens there. Today, the little book where he says it, written as a doorway into Pirkei Avot.
screen: `SWEET TASTES BITTER.` → `A PHYSICIAN'S PICTURE.` → `NOW, THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Shemonah Perakim. Eight Chapters. Maimonides wrote them as an introduction to Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's tractate of sayings about how to live. Before he explains the sayings, he wants you to understand the one who will practice them: the human soul. Take it in steps. First, the soul has health and sickness, just like a body. A healthy soul tends toward good actions and finds them natural. A sick soul tends toward harmful ones, and, like the sick tongue, may even call them sweet. Second, a sick person needs a doctor, and doesn't trust their own cravings. So too, he says, a person whose soul is unwell should go to the wise, who are physicians of souls, and let them help. Third, the cure is practice. Traits are changed the way health is restored: by doing, again and again, until a new habit takes hold. Pirkei Avot, read this way, is a book of medicine. Fourth, where he gathered it. In his introduction he says plainly that these ideas aren't all his own. He drew on the sages and on the philosophers, and he tells the reader to hear the truth from whoever says it. A physician uses the remedy that works, whoever found it. That's the doorway into Avot: not a rulebook, a clinic. The soul's health.

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days: is there a habit of the heart that keeps showing up, impatience, worry, a quick tongue? Don't scold yourself; name it plainly, the way you'd say a knee is sore. Then ask, gently, when it flares up.

1139.title: Maimonides' middle way
1139.hook: virtue lies in the middle between extremes
1139.carry: the middle path is the way of the lord
1139.howItsDone: Jewish teachers of character, in the tradition called mussar, study Maimonides' Laws of Character Traits and the Eight Chapters, and students often work on one trait at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemonah Perakim, the Eight Chapters: a soul can be well or unwell. Your line: the soul's health. Today, the medicine itself.

Somewhere between the person who won't pick up the check and the person who hands out money until there's none left for rent, there's a third person. Generous. Not stingy, not wasteful. Somewhere between the one who freezes at every risk and the one who jumps at all of them, there's another. Brave. Maimonides noticed that good traits seem to live in between. He wrote it in the Eight Chapters, and again in his code of law. Today, the place in between.
screen: `STINGY, WASTEFUL, OR GENEROUS.` → `FROZEN, RECKLESS, OR BRAVE.` → `GOOD TRAITS LIVE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: The middle way. Start with the rule. For almost every trait, Maimonides says, there are two extremes, and both are unhealthy. The good path is the measure in the middle. Not too much, not too little: generous between stingy and wasteful, brave between reckless and timid, content between greedy and careless. Second, he gives this path a name from the Torah. In Genesis, God says Abraham will teach his household to "keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and justice." Maimonides reads the way of the LORD as this middle path. Walking it is a way of walking in God's ways. Third, the cure. If someone has drifted to one extreme, aiming straight for the middle isn't enough. A stingy person, he says, should give generously for a while, even too generously, until the stinginess loosens. Then come back to the middle. A tree bent one way is pulled the other way before it stands straight. Fourth, the warning. Some people, wary of desire, swing to the far opposite: refusing ordinary food and comfort, more than the Torah asks. Maimonides calls that a wrong road too. The Torah, he says, didn't forbid ordinary good things. Holiness doesn't require misery. So the middle isn't lukewarm. It's balanced, and it takes work to stay there, like standing on a moving deck. The middle way.

1140.title: Except anger and pride
1140.hook: for anger and pride he says go far toward the opposite
1140.howItsDone: Students of Jewish ethics study Maimonides' Laws of Character Traits, chapter 2, where he names anger and pride as the exceptions to the middle path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the middle way: good traits between two extremes. Today, the two traits where Maimonides says the middle isn't enough.

"Now the man Moses was very meek." That's a line from the book of Numbers. Maimonides lingers on one word in it. Not meek. Very meek. In his code he teaches that good traits live in the middle, between two extremes. Then, a little further on, he stops and makes an exception. There are a couple of traits, he says, where the middle is still too close to danger. For these, a person should go far, all the way toward the opposite end. Today, the exceptions.
screen: `MOSES WAS VERY MEEK.` → `NOT MEEK. VERY MEEK.` → `WHERE THE MIDDLE ISN'T ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Except anger and pride. Take pride first. With most traits, Maimonides says, aim for the middle. But not here. It isn't enough to be a little humble. A person should be very humble, lowly of spirit, like Moses. That's why the verse says very meek. And he points to the sages in Pirkei Avot, who said it twice over: be very, very humble. Pride, for Maimonides, isn't a trait you can safely keep a little of. Now anger. Anger, he says, is a very bad trait, and here too a person should go far to the other side, training themselves not to get angry even over something that seems to deserve it. He passes on a hard saying of the sages: getting angry is like worshiping idols. In the moment of rage, something else sits on the throne. Then, a practical twist. Sometimes a parent or a leader needs others to take a matter seriously. Maimonides allows them to show anger on the outside, while staying calm within. The face may be stern. The heart stays still. Now step back and look at why these two are the exceptions. Pride and anger both put the self at the center of the room. Most traits can be balanced. These two, he seems to say, tip over too easily, so he keeps them far from the edge. Far from pride.
screen: `PRIDE: NOT A LITTLE HUMBLE. VERY.` · `ANGER: GO FAR TO THE OTHER SIDE.` · `STERN FACE, CALM HEART.` · `BOTH PUT THE SELF AT THE CENTER.` · then, large: `FAR FROM PRIDE.`

Except anger and pride. The two traits where Maimonides says to leave the middle and go far toward the opposite: very humble, and very slow to anger. Today's word.
Your line: far from pride. And far from anger, too, even when it seems deserved. See you tomorrow.

1141.title: Mishneh Torah
1141.hook: a fourteen-book code of all Jewish law in clear Hebrew
1141.howItsDone: The Mishneh Torah is studied in yeshivas and in daily study programs that read it in order, and rabbis consult it alongside later codes; printed editions carry the Ra'avad's critical notes and later commentaries beside the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two exceptions to the middle way. Your line: far from pride. This week walked with Maimonides, from his principles to the soul's health; today, his great code of law.

A king of Israel, the Torah says, must write for himself "a copy of this law" and keep it with him, reading it all the days of his life. In Hebrew, that copy is called mishneh torah. Maimonides took those two words for the name of his code of law. The laws of character from the last two days, the middle way and the far side of anger and pride, come from it. Today, the whole book.
screen: `A KING'S COPY OF THE LAW.` → `MISHNEH TORAH.` → `THE CODE THAT HOLDS IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Mishneh Torah. Maimonides explains the name himself, in his introduction. A person reads the written Torah first, he says, and then reads this book, and from it knows the whole oral law, without needing any other book in between. That's a bold aim, and he says it plainly. First, the language. His commentary on the Mishnah was in Arabic. This time he writes in Hebrew, in the clear Hebrew of the Mishnah, short and direct, so the law can be read without a long argument attached. Second, the order. The Talmud follows its conversations wherever they wander. Maimonides sorts the law by subject instead: prayer with prayer, Shabbat with Shabbat, damages with damages. He divides it into fourteen books, each with its own sections. Third, the reach. He includes everything, even laws no one could keep in his day: the Temple service, the kings, the sacrifices. The whole law, as if it might all be needed again. Fourth, the cost. Because he gives rulings without naming his sources, some rabbis objected. One of them, the Ra'avad, wrote sharp notes against him, and in printed editions those notes sit right beside the text. The code and its critic share the page. This path has met that pattern before: a book of law, and an answer printed next to it. Still, a reader who opens it finds the law laid out from the first page to the last. The whole law in order.
screen: `READ THE TORAH, THEN THIS.` · `CLEAR HEBREW, LIKE THE MISHNAH.` · `SORTED BY SUBJECT, IN FOURTEEN BOOKS.` · `THE CRITIC ON THE SAME PAGE.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE LAW IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Picture a shelf where everything you need is in its place, one subject beside the next, and notice how the body feels when things have an order. Then pick one subject from your own life you'd like to understand better: Shabbat, prayer, charity, food. Rest in that order for a few breaths.
Mishneh Torah. Maimonides' code of Jewish law, in clear Hebrew, sorted by subject into fourteen books, named for the king's copy of the law. Today's word.
Your line: the whole law in order. And a critic printed right beside it. Until tomorrow.
